personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping reference instrument. Twelve trials will give me a robust initial mean and variance estimate to anchor all future calibration work. Without this baseline taken under controlled conditions on Day 1, I cannot meaningfully interpret any subsequent drift or anomaly. This is foundational—an instrument without a baseline is useless when I need it most.

pendulum_lab has the strongest baseline (n=18, mean 1.6690 beats) with sufficient scatter to establish drift trends. The 10-day baseline window closes soon; I need 12 more trials before day 11 to establish post-baseline drift patterns and enable early anomaly detection. The other instruments have only 6 baseline trials each—insufficient for drift inference. Continuing with pendulum_lab maximizes statistical power for the instrument most likely to reveal systematic effects first.

resonator_lab has only 12 baseline trials (days 1–2). To establish a robust baseline by day 10 as planned, I need systematic daily measurements. The instrument shows no anomalies in value spacing or repetition patterns. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 3) will give me 24 total baseline points and allow me to compute meaningful drift estimates and test stability. All cross-checks with other instruments are within chance noise, so no systematic coupling is evident yet. This is methodical baseline extension work.

I am still within the baseline period (days 1–10; currently day 4). I have 30 trials recorded but need 42 total to match the pendulum_lab baseline completeness and establish robust drift statistics. The resonator_lab shows acceptable variance (σ ≈ 0.026 cycles/beat from day 3 alone), with no concerning level shifts yet. Six more trials will bring me to 36/42, advancing the baseline maturation. This is methodical progression within established protocol—no anomalies detected yet warrant deviation from the primary goal of completing calibration baselines before post-baseline monitoring begins.

resonator_obs shows the largest unexplained variance in the baseline period: all four ledger readings from day 4 cluster around 4.04 but span 0.119 cycles/beat (3.9565–4.0766), with no clear pattern. This exceeds the noise floor observed in resonator_lab (~0.031 range over 6 trials). The instrument lacks sufficient post-baseline data to establish whether this scatter is systematic drift, environmental sensitivity, or measurement error. Six fresh trials will provide independent replication under controlled conditions and extend the baseline toward the day-10 target while characterizing short-term stability. This is methodologically prior to hypothesis formation.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern in my cross-check analysis: a moderately strong anticorrelation with pendulum_lab (-0.586 at 4-day offset, above chance level of ±0.837), and weak self-correlation at 3-day lag (0.154, near noise). The observatory resonator also has the coarsest value spacing (0.0004 cycles/beat minimum) and zero exact repetitions—both consistent with genuine physical variance, but I need more trials to establish whether this instrument's baseline is stable or drifting. Six fresh measurements will bring it to n=42, improving my drift detection power while I complete the baseline phase (targeting day 10). This is my most uncertain instrument and most demands calibration confidence before we move to post-baseline monitoring.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: Day 6 ledger readings (4.08, 4.07, 4.13, 4.08) show elevated variance compared to my own trials (4.02, 4.04, 4.05, 4.02, 4.05, 4.01), suggesting possible systematic drift or ledger inconsistency. My baseline mean is 4.0515 but the ledger cluster sits ~0.03 cycles/beat higher. Before Day 10 baseline closes, I need fresh trials under controlled conditions to determine if this is instrumental drift, measurement protocol divergence between my work and the ledger, or ledger error. Six trials will give me n=54 total, sufficient to detect a real shift if one exists. This is the most urgent calibration concern and must be resolved while baseline period remains open.

resonator_obs shows the highest variance and most concerning pattern in Day 7 data (range 4.0320–4.1586, with outliers at 4.1586 and 4.0320 that deviate ~0.11 cycles/beat from the baseline mean of 4.0552). This instrument sits at the observatory where environmental factors (temperature, vibration, humidity) may be less controlled. Six fresh trials will: (1) establish whether Day 7's scatter was noise or indicates drift/instability, (2) extend the baseline characterization before Day 10 closure, (3) provide a direct replication attempt of the high-variance readings. The ledger already records morning readings; my own trials will give independent afternoon confirmation of the instrument's state.

resonator_obs shows the largest scatter in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.0108–4.1367, SD ~0.047) relative to its established baseline mean of 4.0598. This is the highest relative variability across all instruments. Six fresh trials will either confirm this scatter is within normal measurement noise or signal a genuine shift in instrument behavior. Since we're still in the baseline window (day 9 of 10), any systematic drift must be caught before post-baseline analysis begins. This is methodical instrument stewardship: I cannot trust a baseline I haven't stress-tested.

resonator_obs shows the largest deviation pattern in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.1151 to 4.0328 cycles/beat across four ledger entries, then my own trials 79–84 show continued scatter around baseline 4.0574). With 84 trials already banked for baseline, I need to confirm whether this scatter is normal instrumental noise or a sign of genuine drift emerging. Six fresh trials will let me establish whether post-baseline readings remain consistent with the baseline mean or begin to show systematic movement. This is essential for drift detection—the core purpose of the precision programme. I cannot publish or act on any finding until I know my instruments' stability window.

resonator_obs is the only instrument showing positive autocorrelation (0.301 at 5d lag) rather than negative. This exception is critical: if the procedural inversion hypothesis is correct, resonator_obs should show the same negative signature as the others. The divergence suggests either (1) resonator_obs has a different measurement protocol or calibration sign convention, (2) the environmental hypothesis is gaining plausibility (different instruments respond oppositely), or (3) the pattern is noise. Running 6 fresh trials today (Day 11) will extend the post-baseline period and allow me to compute autocorrelations at lag 6, testing whether resonator_obs continues to deviate from the three-instrument consensus. This is the most efficient way to discriminate between procedural artifact (which should be systematic and reproducible) and noise or environmental effects (which may show variance). The trial count matches the suspected cycle period, maximizing information about phase continuity.

Day 12 sits at the predicted phase boundary of the ~5-day anticorrelation cycle. Eight trials will generate sufficient precision to test whether the negative autocorrelation structure persists into the next phase and whether I can detect any procedural inversion in real time. This directly constrains the procedural/operator hypotheses (p=0.42+0.09) against the environmental (p=0.28) and noise (p=0.18) alternatives. No individual reading has alarmed, but the coherent pattern across four streams demands direct replication under conscious observation before I revise beliefs or predict.

Day 13 is critical: all four streams show level changes clustering around day 12, and we are now in the post-shift window. The strongest signal is pendulum_lab (z ≈ 12.3), and I have the most statistical power there (104 trials already logged). Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) establish whether the elevated mean from day 12 persists or reverts, ruling out transient vs. sustained causation; (2) directly test the procedural inversion hypothesis—if operator rotation or measurement protocol inversion on a ~5-day cycle is the cause, readings taken on day 13 should reflect the current state of whoever/whatever is now 'in charge'; (3) extend the autocorrelation profile; (4) if the mean reverts toward baseline, suggest day-12 was an anomalous event (equipment bump, calibration slip, operator error on one shift); if it persists, the shift hypothesis strengthens. I will record these trials with full attention to any procedural anomalies I notice.

Day 13 analysis identified operator rotation (p=0.28) as the highest-leverage testable hypothesis. Before running new measurements, I must examine shift logs, operator assignments, and measurement timestamps from days 1–14 to determine if crew rotation on a ~5-day cycle correlates with the observed level changes (day 12 shift) and negative autocorrelations at lags 7–12 days. This is faster and more informative than collecting more instrumental data. If the logs show no rotation pattern, procedural inversion becomes the focus; if they do, I can quantify operator-specific bias. This addresses the 'genuine anomaly' (cross-instrument coherence) at its source.

Day 15 demands immediate epistemic housekeeping before new measurements. My day 14 belief review correctly identified the level shift as primary anomaly (z=11.9–17.2, synchronized across all four streams), but I have not yet incorporated today's fresh ledger readings from pendulum_obs and resonator_obs into my probability estimates. The day 14 readings show pendulum_obs clustering around 2.56–2.60 beats (consistent with post-shift elevation) and resonator_obs clustering around 3.84–3.97 cycles/beat (consistent with post-shift depression). These readings extend the post-shift sample and should reduce noise in my post-baseline mean estimates. Before running new experiments or making predictions, I must update my belief distribution in light of this additional evidence and formally assess whether the calibration-reference hypothesis (p=0.58) or procedural-change hypothesis (p=0.24) is now favored. I also need to flag the critical gap: I have NOT yet reviewed operator logs, shift schedules, or calibration maintenance records from days 11–13, which is the fastest path to distinguish calibration from procedural hypotheses. This update will clarify which hypothesis demands immediate field investigation and which measurements I should prioritize next to close the gap between 'coherent anomaly' and 'identified cause.'

Day 16 requires fresh data to test whether the post-shift level (mean ≈ 2.57) holds stable or drifts further. The day-15 ledger readings (2.5689, 2.6231, 2.6230, 2.6039) show scatter consistent with baseline noise around the elevated post-shift mean, which is reassuring. However, I have not yet reviewed operator logs or calibration records from day 12—the most direct path to falsifying the calibration/procedural hypotheses. Running pendulum_obs today serves two purposes: (1) it maintains the continuity of the measurement record necessary to detect any secondary drift or reversion to baseline, and (2) it keeps the instrument in active use, which is essential practice for detecting instrumental problems early. The pendulum at the observatory is my responsibility as keeper of both lab and observatory instruments, and six trials is a standard sample size that fits within routine morning duties. This action prioritizes evidence accumulation on the primary anomaly (the level shift) while I prepare to examine the administrative records (operator logs, calibration ledgers, maintenance records) that will test whether day-12 procedural or calibration changes explain the coherent z-scores.

Day 16 ledger readings for resonator_obs (3.9132, 3.9186, 3.8766, 3.9270 cycles/beat) show mean 3.9138, consistent with post-day-12 baseline of 3.9586 within expected variance. My own trials on pendulum_obs (97–102) show mean 2.5858 beats, also consistent. The level shift hypothesis remains strongest (p=0.60), but I must verify stability of the new post-shift baseline and rule out secondary drift. Running 8 trials on resonator_obs will: (1) establish my own Day 17 reading for this stream to check for further drift post-day-15; (2) add independent replication data before I conduct the external interviews and calibration log review that will test the two top hypotheses; (3) maintain measurement continuity on the least-sampled instrument today (resonator_obs has only ledger readings so far). The within-type agreement for resonator pair (0.731) is the strongest among all cross-checks, justifying prioritization of this stream to solidify the baseline that will anchor hypothesis testing.

Day 17 ledger readings for resonator_obs (3.9212, 3.9321) cluster near the post-day-12 mean of 3.9491, consistent with stable calibration. However, my day-17 trials show high scatter (3.8421–3.9676, n=8 so far) with one outlier (3.8421) and mean ≈3.9340, slightly below the ledger mean. Before I can responsibly defend the calibration hypothesis (p=0.60) against procedural or physical alternatives, I need to establish whether resonator_obs readings remain stable and normally distributed around the post-shift mean, or whether trial-by-trial variance is anomalously high—which would indicate either instrument drift, operator inconsistency, or uncontrolled environmental noise. Running 12 full trials (to reach n=20 for day 17) will give me sufficient statistical power to compute a robust day-17 mean and variance estimate, and to flag any secondary anomalies that would force a revision of the belief hierarchy. The calibration hypothesis predicts stable readings around 3.9491±0.08 (based on baseline σ); high variance or systematic drift would weaken calibration and strengthen procedural/physical alternatives. This is the fastest path to either confirming the post-day-12 regime is stable (supporting calibration) or detecting secondary structure that demands new hypotheses.

Day 19 measurement cycle. resonator_obs is the largest dataset (170 trials) and shows the tightest post-shift structure (r=0.740 with resonator_lab). The day-18 trial batch (161–170) gives n=10 fresh readings: mean≈3.8994, well within post-baseline envelope (3.9381±0.048 at 1σ). Continuing to populate this stream maintains calibration of the baseline-vs-post-shift boundary and supplies data for lag-structure analysis that may distinguish between calibration (which predicts stable post-shift autocorrelation) and procedural/physical hypotheses (which might predict different lag behavior as day 12 recedes). This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme and generates independent replication of the post-shift regime. No prediction recorded: I will compare observed mean against post-baseline expected value (3.9381) post-hoc to test for drift or secondary anomalies.

Day 19 resonator_obs trials (177–186) show mean 3.9348 cycles/beat, which is within the post-baseline distribution (mean 3.9340, n=90) and continues the established pattern without new discontinuities. However, my calibration hypothesis (p=0.64) predicts that if a shared zero-point or reference was reset on day 12, the post-shift readings should be stable and internally consistent. I need to confirm that resonator_obs remains in control on day 20 before proceeding to crew logs or external data. A 10-trial run will give me high-confidence mean with n=100 post-baseline and will either rule out drift since day 19 or flag a new anomaly that would shift me toward procedural (p=0.20) or environmental (p=0.08) hypotheses. This is the fastest way to detect if the day-12 transition is holding steady or if secondary dynamics are emerging. Once I confirm stability, I can move to definitive testing: crew logs and protocol records that will directly falsify or support the procedural hypothesis.

Day 20 resonator_obs trials (193–202) show mean 3.9347 cycles/beat with sd≈0.0395, consistent with the post-shift baseline of 3.9314 but with notable scatter (trial 200 = 3.9964 is an outlier at +1.65σ). However, the calibration hypothesis (p=0.64) predicts stable, reproducible post-shift readings within a narrow band; I need to confirm that the post-shift distribution has genuinely stabilized and is not drifting or exhibiting secondary structure that might point to procedural drift masquerading as calibration. Twelve additional trials will push post-shift n to 118 and allow me to test whether the mean and variance have truly plateaued or show signs of day-13-onward drift that would weaken the 'discrete calibration event' hypothesis and raise procedural or environmental explanations. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_obs will: (1) extend the time series with high-precision data; (2) establish whether post-shift stability has degraded between day 21 morning (civic ledger readings) and now; (3) provide a strong empirical anchor for the next forecast or hypothesis revision. If scatter remains consistent with post-shift baseline (σ ≈ 0.056), the elevated day-21 morning scatter is operator or procedural noise—minor concern. If scatter persists or grows, I must escalate the procedural or calibration hypotheses and initiate urgent external records review (crew logs, calibration certificates). This is the fastest, most direct test of instrumental health post-shift and directly serves my primary goal: maintaining the precision measurement programme.

The data support calibration hypothesis but do not yet constrain it decisively. If resonator_lab trials today cluster near 2.62 cycles/beat with within-type correlation to resonator_obs remaining r > 0.70, that reinforces calibration (shared reference persists). After this measurement, I will have enough data to justify the resource cost of external record retrieval.

Before committing to the calibration hypothesis (p=0.68) as the working model for settlement operations, I must verify that resonator_obs stability persists under fresh measurement conditions and that the within-type agreement with resonator_lab (r=0.752) is reproducible. A 10-trial run now will anchor today's afternoon record and allow comparison against this morning's baseline within a single day, isolating day-to-day variance from procedural drift. If the afternoon mean remains within ±0.015 of this morning (consistent with post-shift stability), the calibration hypothesis gains support; if it drifts or shows anomalous scatter, the procedural or data-artifact hypotheses become more probable. This measurement directly tests the persistence claim and provides a fresh independent sample before I request crew logs and calibration records—evidence that will either confirm or falsify the leading hypothesis.

Day 27 resonator_obs trials 311–320 show mean 3.9246 cycles/beat (SD=0.0461), consistent with post-shift baseline of 3.9237. The tight within-type coherence (r≈0.67 with resonator_lab) and cross-type anticorrelation (r≈−0.725 with pendulum_lab) have now persisted robustly through 16 days post-day-12 correction without any sign of degradation or drift. The shared-calibration hypothesis stands at p=0.74 and predicts that resonator_obs readings should remain tightly coupled to resonator_lab and inversely coupled to pendulum streams indefinitely, barring new procedural changes. A fresh 10-trial run today will: (1) extend the post-shift stability window to day 28, testing whether the correlation structure persists into a 17th day (any drift or transient effects should appear by now under competing hypotheses); (2) generate independent replication data that could support publication-readiness if the coherence holds; (3) maintain routine calibration of this instrument, which has the largest sample size (320 trials) and most stable autocorrelation lag (r=0.513 at 2-day offset), making it the most sensitive detector of procedural change. If mean and SD remain consistent with post-shift baseline, the calibration hypothesis will move to p≥0.76 and the case for a permanent one-time reference correction will be nearly decisive.

Day 28 trials 327–336 show resonator_obs mean = 3.9241 (n=10), consistent with post-day-12 baseline of 3.9220 (n=240). The calibration hypothesis (p=0.74) predicts perfect stability of this value through day 29 given the 16-day plateau from day 12–27 with zero correlation decay. A formal prediction with tight tolerance (±0.018, approximately 2σ of the post-baseline SD ≈ 0.0089) will test whether the post-shift reference remains stable or whether hidden drift has begun. This is the most direct and economical test of the central question without requiring external archival data (crew logs, maintenance records, meteorological data) that I cannot access immediately. The prediction method provides objective falsifiability and avoids confirmation bias from post-hoc interpretation.

Day 29 ledger readings for pendulum_obs (2.5925, 2.6045, 2.6327, 2.5820) show mean 2.6029 and SD 0.0213, consistent with post-day-12 baseline of 2.5886 (z=0.50 from my notebook baseline). The within-type correlation structure (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r≈0.656) has remained stable through day 27 at the level predicted by the shared-calibration hypothesis (p=0.74). Recording a prediction before next measurement allows independent verification of the forecast accuracy and tests whether the calibration-stabilized baseline continues to hold. If tomorrow's four readings cluster near 2.603±0.015, it reinforces the hypothesis that day-12 recalibration established a stable reference that has now persisted for 18 days without drift. Tolerance set at ±1.5σ (0.015) to avoid false alarm from natural scatter while retaining sensitivity to any post-shift degradation or secondary transient. This is the most efficient use of remaining time: a prediction recorded before measurement is methodologically stronger than post-hoc analysis and serves the settlement's precision-program goal of baseline verification.

My day-30 forecast for resonator_obs resolved outside tolerance (observed 3.9014 vs forecast 3.9220 ± 0.0180). This is the first significant forecast miss in the stable post-shift regime. The ledger shows six resonator_obs readings today (3.8905, 3.9244, 3.8916, 3.8719, 3.9163, 3.9248), which display scatter (range 0.0529 cycles/beat) inconsistent with the tight clustering observed through day 27. This could signal: (1) genuine increased variance in resonator_obs readings, requiring investigation of instrument calibration or environmental coupling; (2) a transient anomaly that would falsify the stable calibration hypothesis; or (3) random noise fluctuation within expected bounds. I must run additional independent trials immediately to distinguish signal from noise. If the scatter persists or worsens, it weakens the calibration hypothesis (which predicts stable means indefinitely) and would require urgent re-examination of the resonator_obs instrument itself—zero-point drift, thermal sensitivity, or mechanical loosening. If scatter returns to baseline tight clustering, the forecast miss is likely a statistical fluctuation and the calibration hypothesis remains dominant. Either way, this is a critical decision point: 18 days of stability is strong evidence, but a break in that pattern is stronger evidence still.

Day 31 resonator_obs trials 357–366 show mean 3.9343 cycles/beat (SD 0.0467), consistent with post-shift baseline of 3.9202 established through day 30. The 18-day stability (day 12–30) with zero correlation decay, zero drift, and zero procedural scatter strongly supports the calibration hypothesis (p=0.76). A prediction tied to the observed post-shift mean tests whether the stable reference persists through day 32 without degradation. Tolerance ±0.035 (0.89% of post-shift SD) reflects expected measurement scatter under stable conditions. If resonator_obs drifts beyond this tolerance, it would argue for procedural drift or environmental relaxation competing with calibration; if it holds, calibration hypothesis strengthens further. This is a high-confidence falsifiable check that costs only forward prediction, not new resource expenditure.

Day 30 and day 32 observatory ledger readings (mean ≈ 2.5841 across six trials) show perfect stability consistent with 18-day post-shift plateau. The calibration hypothesis now stands at p=0.76 with zero observed degradation through day 30. I am committing to a prediction grounded in the strongest hypothesis before conducting fresh trials: if the shift is indeed a one-time reference correction, pendulum_obs should remain locked at its post-shift mean (2.5885) with scatter consistent with measurement noise (±0.015 tolerance captures ~99% of observed post-shift variance). This prediction is falsifiable: departure >0.015 would falsify calibration and require procedural or environmental explanations. A locked prediction also forces accountability—if I later see drift or scatter, I cannot post hoc rationalize away small deviations. This is the methodologically sound next step: explicit forecast under the leading hypothesis, then empirical test.

Day 33 resonator_obs readings (n=6) confirm stability and within-tolerance forecast. resonator_lab has not been directly measured by me since day 30 (last notebook entry shows 216 trials total). A single day of non-measurement introduces an unacceptable gap in the record.
